Gagaku is Japan's ancient imperial court music, performed continuously for over twelve hundred years. A refined ensemble tradition, it features winds including the shawm and flute, alongside strings like the koto and biwa, and percussion instruments. The music is organized into instrumental dances and processional pieces that marked state ceremonies, religious rites, and entertainment for the imperial household.

Gagaku originated as a fusion of Japanese indigenous music, Tang Dynasty Chinese music, and Korean and Central Asian influences. Each layer left distinct stylistic traces that remain identifiable in the repertoire. The ensembles feature the sho, a free-reed mouth organ, the ryuteki transverse flute, and the hichiriki, a double-reed shawm. These are paired with the koto, a long zither, and the biwa, a plucked lute. Percussion includes drums and gongs that anchor the ensemble.

Pieces are organized into three categories. Bugaku consists of instrumental dances with masked dancers. Kangen refers to purely instrumental versions of the same works. Roei comprises vocal pieces accompanied by instruments. Many pieces bear Chinese titles and were adopted from Tang court tradition. The repertoire includes works over a millennium old, preserved through strict oral transmission from master to student.

The imperial court maintains an official gagaku ensemble that performs at state ceremonies. Transmission is jealously guarded, with apprenticeship beginning in childhood. Gagaku is unlike many Asian music traditions in that it was never significantly interrupted. It is the world's oldest continuously practiced court music ensemble tradition. Modern performances evoke an austere, meditative aesthetic. The slow tempo and timbral subtlety demand intense listener concentration.
